definition: Underling means a person of lower rank who carries out orders.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word underling. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know underling should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Every complaint reaches the minister already softened, filtered upward through three layers of underlings.
Assistant is respectful — a title a person puts on a résumé — while underling is the view from above: not a colleague, just someone to send.
Lackey drops below even underling: an underling merely ranks low and obeys, while a lackey has traded self-respect for the job, fetching and flattering on command.

A minion serves a powerful figure eagerly, almost devotedly — half follower, half fan — and the villain's minions are proud of the job. Underling drops the eagerness: it names anyone whose whole role is taking orders, and the sneer belongs to the boss looking down, not the servant looking up.

A flunky is kept around for errands and flattery — carrying coats, laughing at jokes — useful mainly for being agreeable. An underling holds a real place in a real chain of command; the contempt in underling is about low rank, while the contempt in flunky is about servility.

Underling means a person of lower rank who carries out orders.
The fashion house's founder swept through the atelier trailing underlings: one carried her coffee, one her sketchbook, one simply nodded at whatever she said.
None of them, the staff joked, had heard their own names in years — she called them all 'you.'

Underling does the sneering that 'assistant' politely refuses to do: it names someone whose whole role is to take orders from above, and it looks down on them from the speaker's height while doing so.
Underling is never neutral: use it to convey that the powerful person sees faceless, swappable order-takers, not colleagues — or to accuse them of seeing exactly that.
On a résumé the same person is an assistant; in the villain's monologue, a minion.
Its natural partner in this unit is subordinate, the org chart's cold but respectful adjective for the same position.

For six years, Marisol Vega ran the logistics floor of Harlan Freight in everything but title.
To the executives upstairs, though, she remained an underling: someone to send for files, someone whose name appeared on no memo, someone the directors stepped past in the elevator without a nod.
When the port strike hit, the upstairs men drafted three plans that collapsed in a week.
Marisol's routing scheme, passed upward through her supervisor, kept the trucks moving for a month.
The board finally asked who had written it.
The answer embarrassed them: the fix had come from three ranks below, from a person none of them could have picked out of the lobby.
